en: The Jātaka:
The Section of Eleven, Chapter on the Supporter of His Mother.
1. The Mātuposaka Jātaka “During the absence of that nāga,
the sallakī and kuṭaja trees grew tall.”
Kuruvindas, karavīras, abhisas, and sāmās,
and kanikāra trees blooming in the windless stillness;
and here and there, golden armlets.
They support the Naga king with alms-food,
so that wherever the king or a prince shall advance unafraid, he will be clad in armor.
“Take a morsel, O Naga;
do not be emaciated, O Naga.
There are many royal duties [to be performed].”
“Will you not do those things, O Nāga?
“Surely she is a wretched woman,
blind and without a guide.”
“He stirs up a stump with his foot and causes a mountain with fierce lions to fall.
“Who indeed is that one for you, O Great Naga?”
Blind and without a guide,
she stumbles against a stump with her foot and falls into a mountain ravine filled with fierce lions.
“O Great King, she was my mother,
blind and without a guide;
she would strike against a stump with her foot.”
"Release this great elephant, who supports his mother, as he falls toward the mountain Caṇḍoraṇa."
“Let the Naga meet with his mother and with all his kinsmen.
“The Naga is released from his bonds;”
Taking up his urine,
the elephant comforted him for a moment and then went toward the mountain.
Then, having gone to that lotus pond frequented by elephants,
he drew up cool water with his trunk.
“Sprinkle water upon your mother!
“Who is this ignoble deity who rains even out of season?”
“My own son has gone away, he who was my attendant.
“Arise, mother! Why do you lie there?”
"I am a kinsman come here;
I have been released by the illustrious King of Kāsi, the Videhan."
“May that king live long,
the increaser of the kingdom of Kāsi,
who has released my son.”
"Always honoring the Buddha.
Thus ends the first Jātaka, the Mātuposaka-jātaka.
